title: Occasion: Dartmouth's appointment, 1772
short: Celebrates the appointment of William Legge, 2nd Earl of Dartmouth, as Secretary of State for the Colonies in August 1772.
body: Dartmouth (1731-1801) succeeded the unpopular Earl of Hillsborough as Secretary of State for the American colonies on 27 August 1772. Colonists hoped he would be conciliatory, since as President of the Board of Trade in 1765-66 he had been associated with the ministry that repealed the Stamp Act. He was also an evangelical, a supporter of the Methodist movement and connected with the circle of the Countess of Huntingdon, Wheatley's patron; Dartmouth College was named for him. Wheatley sent the poem with a letter dated 10 October 1772, transmitted by the merchant Thomas Wooldridge, and revised it for the 1773 Poems.

anchor: Fair Freedom rose New-England to adorn
title: Freedom as goddess
short: Freedom is personified as a dawn goddess rising over New England; the whole poem turns on the word.
body: Wheatley imagines Freedom as a sunrise, 'smiling like the morn', a figure close to Aurora. In colonial political language 'freedom' meant relief from parliamentary 'tyranny', and the poem uses it in that sense first. Its later stanzas reapply the word to the slave trade and to her own capture, so that the colonists' cry for liberty is turned back on them. Critics such as Carretta and Shields see this double application as the poem's central strategy.

title: genial
short: Life-giving, warming, favourable to growth; the older sense, from Latin genialis.
body: Latin genialis meant 'of generation or birth', and hence festive or fruitful. In eighteenth-century poetic usage 'genial' rays are those of the sun that make things grow. The 'northern clime' of New England, often described as cold, is imagined as warmed into life by the new minister's favour. The word links the political compliment to the sunrise image of the opening lines.

title: The silken reins
short: Gentle government: Dartmouth holds the reins of colonial administration lightly, unlike the 'iron chain' of tyranny.
body: The image of government as a charioteer's reins is classical; Wheatley makes them 'silken' to signal mild, consensual rule. The softness contrasts pointedly with the 'iron chain' of l. 17, which the colonists feared from Parliament and which, in the next stanza, becomes literal for the enslaved. The chariot imagery returns at the poem's end with the 'fiery coursers' of Elijah, so that the poem begins and ends with horses and reins.

title: hated faction
short: Usually read as the hostile policy or party associated with Dartmouth's predecessor Hillsborough, which 'languish'd and expir'd' at Freedom's rising.
body: 'Faction' in eighteenth-century politics meant a self-interested party acting against the public good. Wheatley does not name it. Editors generally take it as the ministerial interest identified with the Earl of Hillsborough, whose harsh American policy colonists resented; some readers take it more broadly as any partisan enemy of liberty. The personified faction sickens and dies 'at the view' of the goddess, a mock-epic touch, and the owl simile that follows treats it as a creature of darkness fleeing the dawn.

anchor: The owl in sadness seeks the
title: The owl
short: A simile: faction flees Freedom as the owl, bird of night, retreats from the dawn.
body: The owl was a conventional emblem of darkness, ill omen and obscurantism, and its flight from daylight a familiar simile in Augustan verse. The couplet rounds off the first verse paragraph by returning to the sunrise of l. 1. It also contributes to the poem's pattern of light and darkness, which Wheatley later turns to her own transport from Africa.

sources.cite: Phillis Wheatley, Complete Writings, ed. Vincent Carretta (Penguin Classics, 2001), explanatory notes

title: The triplet and the iron chain
short: A three-line rhyme (strain/complain/chain) marks the colonists' grievance; 'chain' and 'enslave' anticipate the turn to literal slavery.
body: This short paragraph breaks the run of couplets with a triplet, a Drydenian device used for emphasis. Its political metaphor was everywhere in the revolutionary press: colonists described parliamentary taxation as 'slavery' and 'chains'. 'Wanton' means unrestrained or capricious. Wheatley adopts the figure faithfully, but by placing it immediately before her account of being 'snatch'd' from Africa she makes the metaphor confront the fact, a juxtaposition critics regard as quietly pointed.

anchor: from whence my love of Freedom
title: The turn to herself
short: The poet anticipates the earl's surprise and explains where her love of freedom comes from: her own experience.
body: The address 'my lord' and the imagined question ('Wonder from whence...') set up the autobiographical passage that follows, the only place in the 1773 volume where Wheatley speaks directly of her capture. The appeal to 'feeling hearts' draws on the eighteenth-century culture of sensibility, in which the capacity to feel others' pain was a moral credential. The passage thus claims authority for the young African woman to speak about liberty to a minister of state.

title: Afric's fancy'd happy seat
short: Africa, her homeland; 'fancy'd' may mean 'imagined' (an idealised Africa) or 'cherished', and critics differ on its tone.
body: 'Afric' is the poetic form of Africa; 'seat' means dwelling place. 'Fancy'd' is ambiguous: it can mean 'supposed, merely imagined', so that the happiness of Africa is a European fiction or a child's memory, or 'loved, delighted in'. Coupled with 'seeming cruel fate', which hints that providence brought her to Christianity, the line can be read as cautiously keeping faith with her evangelical audience. Other readers stress that the line nonetheless names Africa as a home and her removal as a wrong.

title: excruciating; molest
short: Torturing pains (Latin cruciare, to crucify) must have troubled her parents; 'molest' means distress, afflict.
body: 'Excruciating', from Latin excruciare, 'to torment', built on crux, 'cross', carries a faint Passion overtone appropriate to a devotional poet. 'Molest' had the general sense 'to trouble, vex'. Strikingly the speaker imagines her parents' grief rather than her own,; the passage is often cited as a rare glimpse of the family she lost when she was taken as a child of about seven or eight.

title: 'Such, such my case'
short: Her seizure from her father is offered as the root of her wish that no one else should 'feel tyrannic sway'.
body: The 'steel'd' soul unmoved by misery is the slave trader who tore a child from her father. The repeated 'Such, such' is emphatic and the question that follows is a litotes: she cannot but pray that others be spared tyranny. Read alongside the preceding 'iron chain', the passage extends the colonists' language of political slavery to chattel slavery itself. Critics differ on how strong an antislavery statement this is: some, following Gates and Carretta, see it as a deliberate rebuke to slaveholding patriots; others note its tactful indirection and its framing as a personal prayer.

title: 'Favours past'
short: Probably recalls Dartmouth's earlier association with the repeal of the Stamp Act (1766), and asks him to renew such kindness.
body: The 'favours past' and the griefs 'which thou did'st once deplore' are usually taken to refer to Dartmouth's tenure as President of the Board of Trade in 1765-66, when the Rockingham ministry repealed the Stamp Act, a measure colonists celebrated. The plural 'our thanks' speaks for the colonists collectively; the poet now addresses him as a public spokesperson rather than as an individual sufferer.

title: refulgent fane
short: A shining temple: 'fane' (Latin fanum) is poetic diction for a temple or shrine; 'refulgent' means brilliantly radiant.
body: Both words are Latinate poetic diction: 'fane' from fanum, a consecrated place, and 'refulgent' from refulgere, to shine back. Heaven is imagined as a radiant temple to which Dartmouth will be conducted, a fitting destination for a man celebrated for his piety. The phrase shows the classical vocabulary Wheatley drew from Pope. The temple-and-chariot imagery of the last lines gives the poem a ceremonial, almost apotheotic close, of the kind Pope used in his panegyrics.

anchor: like the prophet, thou shalt find
title: The prophet Elijah
short: Dartmouth is to be carried to heaven in a chariot of fire, like Elijah in 2 Kings 2:11.
body: In 2 Kings 2:11 'there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire' and Elijah 'went up by a whirlwind into heaven'. Wheatley's 'fiery coursers' sweeping 'th' ethereal plain' combine that scene with classical images of the sun's horses. The closing wish that Dartmouth gain immortality not only through 'fleeting Fame' but through heavenly reward is a standard Christian turn in panegyric, apt for an evangelical statesman. The horses also complete the poem's frame of reins and chariots begun in l. 8.

title: Two versions
short: The text sent to Dartmouth in 1772 differs from the printed 1773 version; editors such as Mason and Carretta print or record both.
body: Wheatley regularly revised her poems between manuscript, newspaper and book. The Massachusetts Historical Society holds a manuscript copy, not in Wheatley's hand, of her covering letter of 10 October 1772. Comparing the manuscript text with the printed one shows her revising the poem for publication. Students quoting the poem should note which version they are using; this archive gives the 1773 book text.
